transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-17 | 16:00 PDT start | Duration ~78 min
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jon Lee (Redwood Eng), Alex Chu (CTO, FinEdge), María Gomez (Lead ML), Tariq Hassan (Infra), Eve Park (Security)

[00:00] Samir (Redwood): okay welcome everyone, thanks for hopping on. we scheduled an hour and a bit to walk through the tail latency you're seeing with private vpc deployment, specifically the KV cache hit/miss behavior and network egress affinity. quick intros?
[00:10] Alex (FinEdge): hi all, Alex here. quick thing - we've got consistent spikes at p95 around 420ms and p99s up to 1.2s when traffic mixes multi-tenant requests through our egress nat. wondering if sticky sessions would help.
[00:22] Priya (Redwood): yeah, hi Alex, María, Tariq. we've looked at the traces you shared - some of the p99s correlate with KV cache misses and also with TCP retransmits after MTU fragmentation. we'll unpack both.
[00:35] María (FinEdge): to add, quantized model variant also shows slightly higher variance on some prompt shapes — int8 path is good avg but heavier tail occasionally.
[00:45] Jon (Redwood): for background, our runtime does continuous batching and KV cache is used for prefix reuse across sessions; if requests get routed to different worker nodes due to lack of affinity we see more KVM cold starts.
[01:00] Tariq (FinEdge): right - we do autoscaling and our lb distributes round-robin; NAT egress is an AWS NAT gateway and we have a privatelink-ish peering to the cluster in another account. not classic PrivateLink, but cross-account privatelink with transit.
[01:20] Samir: ok let's go through a simple scenario: client sends stream requests A and B, if they land on different inference workers, KV cache hit rate drops and you pay the cold kv fetch plus cache fill latency. how often are you seeing same-user flows getting different ENIs? Tariq?
[01:38] Tariq: it's sketchy - because we use shared NAT, the source IP is the NAT, not pod. internal ELB has connection affinity for 5 minutes but outbound can hairpin through NAT gateway and source translation causes different backend routing on return, so session stickiness breaks when we scale down/up.
[01:58] Priya: that's classic sticky break. two levers: preserve client source at the L4 LB (preserve source IP) or implement application-level session affinity (session tokens routed by our proxy/router). both have tradeoffs.
[02:15] Alex: preserving source IP isn't possible with our managed transit setup without touching firewall and the shared nat. can we do any smart fallback?
[02:24] Priya: yes - we can implement a short-lived sticky token managed by the SDK in the client. on each request it includes an affinity header, we route requests with the same token to the same worker for e.g., 30s or 60s window. that keeps KV cache hot for a session.
[02:40] María: how does that interplay with batching? if we pin too long we reduce packing efficiency, right?
[02:48] Jon: correct — there's tradeoff. more aggressive affinity reduces KV misses but can reduce batch fill rates. we suggest 200-400ms batching windows for high qps endpoints and 30s sticky windows for chat-like sessions where KV reuse yields big token savings.
[03:05] Alex: in our profiling the KV cache hit gives 60-80ms benefit on p95, so it's worth it for our user flows (long chat).
[03:14] Samir: good note. next network topic: NAT hairpinning and asymmetric routing. Tariq, you mentioned packet captures show RSTs and retransmits?
[03:24] Tariq: yes intermittently. when container egress goes to nat then back into cross-account privatelink, we see TTL differences and occasional path MTU black-holing when jumbo frames are on-prem. some clients use 9000 MTU on-prem but intermediate NAT lowers it, and DF bit plus ICMP unreachable doesn't always propagate.
[03:45] Priya: MTU mismatch is super common. runtime's tokenized payloads can cross an MTU boundary for streaming frames; if you get fragmentation and one fragment lost, you pay a full retransmit which shows up as p99 spike. mitigation: set path MTU discovery fallbacks, enforce 1500 MTU across the chain, or adjust TCP MSS on tunnel endpoints.
[04:05] Eve (FinEdge): we can't change some transit MTU policies due to legacy appliances. is there an application workaround?
[04:13] Jon: yes — we can reduce TCP MSS on the sidecars/ENI to keep segments under 1400 bytes, and enable runtime-level chunking so streaming frames are smaller. also enable keepalive to prevent cold flows from resetting.
[04:28] María: you mentioned DNS timeouts earlier — we saw a cluster where resolver timeouts doubled p95 for cold workers. is that separate?
[04:35] Priya: often related. If a worker is scaled down and cold-start needs to fetch keys or contact KMS or model registry using DNS, slow resolver plus repeated attempts amplify tail. keep a local resolver cache and increase resolver redundancy. also prefer IPs for known services in pilot if possible.
[04:53] Alex: on KMS calls we did see up to 200ms latency on certain regions during key rotation. can we cache key material?
[04:59] Jon: we cache decrypted model keys in memory with TTL aligned to rotation. but initial KMS decrypt can add latency on cold start; for POC we can pre-warm workers or use an encrypted disk with keys loaded at startup.
[05:14] Samir: switching to quantization and kernel choices — María said int8 path had heavier tail. can you explain?
[05:21] Priya: sure. quantized kernels (int8/int4) often rely on different GEMM kernels than fp16. some int8 backends sample-run using specialized int8 kernels that are optimized for throughput but have less deterministic latency due to mixed precision fallback on certain sequence lengths. and on certain CUDA driver versions we saw occasional kernel fallback which causes a 100-300ms spike.
[05:42] Jon: we recommend pinned driver/kernel combos; our runtime supports kernel selection table that picks the lowest tail-latency kernel for your seq-len distribution. for FinEdge, we should run a per-sequence-length latency sweep to pick best quant profile.
[05:58] María: how heavy is the overhead to switch kernels? can't change midstream right?
[06:04] Priya: kernel selection happens at startup/per-model-shard level. switching midstream isn't safe. so we want to find the best kernel once per rollout. that means measuring tail across your target prompts.
[06:18] Alex: ok. practical ask — can Redwood run a benchmark using our 2k prompt sample and show p50/p95/p99 for fp16, int8, int4 with and without sticky sessions?
[06:27] Samir: yes that's an explicit next step. we'll do that and include KV hit/miss breakdown.
[06:33] Tariq: from infra side, what about SNI and mTLS on private links — do those affect latency? we have mTLS between accounts.
[06:41] Jon: mTLS adds small CPU overhead for handshake; once session is established it's negligible. the handshake on cold connect costs 30-80ms depending on cipher and CPU. reuse connections and set TLS session tickets to lengthen reuse. SNI itself doesn't add meaningful time.
[06:58] Eve: security - audit logs and KMS integration. if we enable KMS log export to SIEM, do we see any perf impact?
[07:05] Priya: no, logging is async. the only impact is if you synchronously call an external auditor as part of the request path — we don't do that. keep audits asynchronous.
[07:14] Samir: moving to specific lab proposals — we'll test three configs: 1) baseline (your current LB + shared NAT), 2) app-affinity sticky token, 3) preserve-source-IP at LB + ENI mapping. we'll measure p50/p95/p99, KV hit-rate, batch fill rate, and packet-level retransmits. target window 1 hour each under synthetic load.
[07:39] Alex: good. what's realistic throughput per-worker with quantized int8 and 256-token average?
[07:45] Jon: depends on GPU; on an A10G-like instance with our runtime int8 we see 80-120 tokens/sec per GPU for concurrent streams; batching at 256 tokens and continuous batching can push higher throughput. single-request latencies p50 in 30-60ms range if KV hit and no network tail. p95 numbers tilt higher with misses.
[08:06] María: the 80-120 tokens/sec is fine. our concern is tail when user bursts plus autoscale churn.
[08:13] Priya: autoscale churn you can reduce with scale-in grace (drain connections) and use pre-warm buffer instances. also set cooldowns to avoid thrash.
[08:23] Tariq: cron scaling during business hours caused many ON/OFF cycles. we'll increase min instances.
[08:28] Samir: great. concrete action: Priya will assemble a reproducible KV-hit-rate benchmark harness; we need your sample prompts and network topology. we'll run the sticky-token experiments and NAT hairpin MTU tests. expected output: CSV with timestamps, p50/p95/p99, kv-hit-rate, batch fill rate, packet retransmit counts.
[08:52] Alex: can we get recommended SDK changes for affinity header? we prefer minimal client change.
[08:58] Jon: SDK change is small — add an affinity token returned in initial session create, stored in cookie/local cache, and reused for lifetime. header name we suggest: X-Redwood-Affinity. default TTL 30s, configurable by server. we can also implement transparent proxy-based affinity if you want zero-client changes but that needs load balancer config.
[09:20] María: any gotchas on sticky sessions with multi-region failover? if worker goes down we should fallback to a compatible model variant.
[09:27] Priya: yes. our routing honors model-compatibility matrices. if affinity target fails we'll route to fallback with KV miss penalty; also keep a fallback token TTL to allow immediate re-affinity when the worker returns.
[09:41] Samir: ok time check - 10 minutes left. quick recap of risks: MTU fragmentation, nat hairpin causing asymmetric routes, DNS/KMS cold-starts, kernel selection for quantized paths, and batch/affinity tradeoffs.
[09:57] Alex: sounds right. any recommended immediate config changes?
[10:02] Priya: enable short affinity token in SDK and reduce MSS on sidecars as stopgap. also set resolver cache TTL higher and pin KMS endpoints where possible.
[10:12] Tariq: we'll get pcap and topology by Tue and enable packet capture this weekend for 1 hour.
[10:18] Samir: Samir will send pilot pricing and SE-run lab schedule. Priya will prepare the harness. Jon will draft SDK affinity header spec.
[10:26] Alex: thanks everyone. one last Q — do you have a template for the CSV outputs?
[10:30] Priya: yes we'll include columns: ts, request_id, worker_id, model_variant, seq_len, kv_hit_bool, batch_size, p50,p95,p99, retransmit_count, path_mtu, resolver_latency_ms.
[10:44] Samir: perfect. wrap up. thanks all.

End of transcript.
